items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water in plants.

rubric.why: Identifies the pull generated by transpiration and the water-conducting tissue.
rubric.description: Transpiration from the leaves creates a pulling force in the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transpiration pull with upward movement through xylem.

rubric.why: Cohesion keeps the water column unbroken.
rubric.description: Cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for cohesion maintaining the continuous water column.

rubric.why: Adhesion helps the water column cling to the xylem walls.
rubric.description: Adhesion between water and xylem walls supports the water column.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing adhesion to the xylem walls.

rubric.why: Water loss from leaves initiates the tension that pulls water upward.
rubric.description: Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces produces tension (transpiration pull).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining how water loss from leaves generates tension.

rubric.why: Completes the account of the direction and passive nature of water transport.
rubric.description: The tension pulls water upward from roots towards leaves, without direct expenditure of energy by the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating upward movement from roots to leaves and its passive nature.

modelAnswer: Water evaporates from the leaf surfaces and exits mainly through the stomata, producing transpiration pull or tension.
This tension pulls water upward through the xylem from the roots towards the leaves.
Cohesion between water molecules keeps them joined in a continuous column.
Adhesion between water molecules and the xylem walls helps support this column.
Thus, water is transported upward as a continuous column without direct expenditure of energy by the plant.

items.followUp: What is bioinformatics, and how does it help biological research?

rubric.why: Gives the molecular scope of the field.
rubric.description: Molecular biology is the study of biological processes at the molecular level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the study of biology at the molecular level.

rubric.why: Names the molecules or processes that form its subject matter.
rubric.description: It studies molecules such as DNA and proteins and their roles in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming DNA, proteins, or another relevant biological molecule.

modelAnswer: Molecular biology is the branch of biology that studies life processes at the molecular level.
It studies biological molecules such as DNA and proteins and how they function in living organisms.

items.followUp: What is the organ level of organization? Give one example.

rubric.why: Defines the organization of cells into a functional tissue.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a particular function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining tissue as a group of cells performing a function.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a tissue.
rubric.description: A valid example is muscle tissue, xylem, phloem, or epithelial tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct tissue example.

modelAnswer: The tissue level is a level of organization in which a group of similar cells work together to perform a particular function.

items.followUp: What are quantitative observations? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Distinguishes qualitative observations from measurements expressed as numbers.
rubric.description: Qualitative observations describe qualities or features and are not expressed numerically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that qualitative observations are descriptive and non-numerical.

rubric.why: Recognizes appropriate examples of observed qualities.
rubric.description: Examples include colour, smell, texture, or shape.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one or more valid examples.

modelAnswer: Qualitative observations describe qualities or features without using numerical measurements.
Examples include the colour, smell, texture, or shape of an object.

items.followUp: Why is a control group important in an experiment?

rubric.why: Identifies how the control group differs from the experimental group.
rubric.description: A control group is kept under normal conditions or is not exposed to the tested variable or treatment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the group is not given the experimental treatment or variable.

rubric.why: States the purpose of the control group in interpreting results.
rubric.description: It provides a basis for comparison to determine the effect of the tested variable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it is used for comparison.

modelAnswer: A control group is kept under normal conditions and is not exposed to the experimental variable or treatment.
It is used for comparison with the experimental group to determine the effect of that variable.

items.followUp: Where may ribosomes be found in a cell, and what do they make?

rubric.why: Identifies ribosomes as cell structures and/or gives their location.
rubric.description: Ribosomes are small cell structures found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ribosomes as small structures or giving a correct location.

rubric.why: States the principal function of ribosomes.
rubric.description: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ribosomes make proteins.

modelAnswer: Ribosomes are small cell structures found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum.

rubric.why: Identifies the substance that passes through the membrane.
rubric.description: Reverse osmosis involves water (the solvent) passing through a semipermeable membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water or solvent as the substance that moves.

rubric.why: Describes the membrane and the pressure or direction that makes the process reverse osmosis.
rubric.description: Pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated solution, forcing water through a semipermeable membrane in the reverse direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the applied pressure condition and the membrane or reverse direction.

modelAnswer: Reverse osmosis is the movement of water through a semipermeable membrane in the direction opposite to natural osmosis.
It occurs when pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the concentrated solution, forcing water through the membrane.

items.followUp: State two characteristics of fungi and two characteristics of bacteria.

rubric.why: States a key characteristic of algae.
rubric.description: Algae are generally photosynthetic and contain chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying algae as chlorophyll-containing, photosynthetic, or autotrophic.

rubric.why: Additional relevant characteristic of algae.
rubric.description: Algae may be unicellular or multicellular and are commonly found in aquatic environments.
rubric.how: This point is included in the model answer but does not receive a separate mark.

rubric.why: States a defining characteristic of protozoans.
rubric.description: Protozoans are unicellular organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protozoans as unicellular.

rubric.why: Additional relevant characteristic of protozoans.
rubric.description: Protozoans are generally heterotrophic; many move using cilia, flagella, or pseudopodia.
rubric.how: This point is included in the model answer but does not receive a separate mark.

modelAnswer: Algae are generally photosynthetic organisms containing chlorophyll; they may be unicellular or multicellular and are commonly aquatic.
Protozoans are unicellular and generally heterotrophic; many move using cilia, flagella, or pseudopodia.
